phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial [m], open [a], trilled or tapped r.
Voiced velar [ɡ] and voiced lateral [l]; the name is not Slavic in formation — it is a worn-down loan from the Iranian Simurgh.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SEE-mar-gl' — three quick syllables; a Slavic tongue shaped the foreign name until it could be declined.

kin.label: Iranian
kin.form: Avestan Sīmurγ, Middle Persian Sēnmurw, New Persian Simurgh — the divine bird of Iranian tradition; Simargl is the Simurgh transplanted

kin.label: Proposed
kin.form: an Indic formation śyena-mārga 'eagle-hound' has been aired in the literature; the loan-path via Sarmatian-Alanic steppe peoples is the standard account (Abaev)

kin.label: Slavic adaptation
kin.form: the final -gl shows the folk re-shaping that turned Simurgh into a declinable Slavic theonym

pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Simargl preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses; the temple stands at Tier 2. The name's Iranian origin is among the most secure facts about this figure.

domains.title: Simargl
domains.subtitle: Winged Guardian
domains.lead: Simargl is the strangest god in the Kyiv pantheon: a name borrowed from the Iranian Simurgh, worn smooth by Slavic tongues, standing sixth among Vladimir's idols in 988 with no story, no oath, and no gloss to say what he did. Scholars have made him a guardian of seeds and plant life by inference; the sources themselves are silent.

cards.name: The Idols
cards.desc: One of the six gods of Kyiv drowned in the Dnieper in 988, listed without comment by the Primary Chronicle.

cards.name: Iranian Wings
cards.desc: His name is the Simurgh of Persian epic — a loan carried north by steppe contact, like amber carried by rivers.

cards.name: Guardian of Seeds?
cards.desc: Rybakov's influential hypothesis made him protector of sown fields — a reconstruction, not an attestation.

cards.name: The Silent One
cards.desc: No oath, gloss, festival, or folk name survives — the least documented god of the six.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: From the Simurgh lineage: the composite winged guardian of Iranian iconography, adapted to Slavic soil

symbols.name: Grain and seed
symbols.meaning: Under Rybakov's hypothesis, the sprouting seed he guards against the chthonic adversary

symbols.name: Lion's paws, dog's head
symbols.meaning: The Simurgh's composite body — part dog, part lion, part bird — carried inside the loanword's meaning

symbols.name: Fire on the hill
symbols.meaning: The 980 sacrifices on Kyiv's hill included him; whatever received the offering, flame was its medium

mythology.lead: Simargl has no mythology in the ordinary sense — no tale was ever told about him. He exists as a single line in a chronicle, a name of Iranian ancestry, and a century of scholarly argument about what a winged guardian was doing in a Slavic pantheon.

myths.title: The Idols in the Dnieper
myths.text: In 988 the Primary Chronicle's procession of drowned gods includes, between Stribog and Mokosh, a name no Slavic tongue built: Simargl. The chronicler lists him without curiosity, one idol among six, but modern scholarship has never been able to leave him alone — because his name betrays a long journey, from the Iranian Simurgh, through the speech of steppe peoples who traded and raided along the Black Sea, into the capital of Christianizing Rus'. A pantheon is a nation's self-portrait; Kyiv's included a god borrowed from Persia's. The chronicle line is the whole dossier: no oath, no gloss, no sorcerer, no saint. One drowning, recorded by the enemies who arranged it — and a foreign accent still audible in the name as it went under. No later source ever asked who had carried him there; only modern scholarship heard the accent at all.

myths.title: A Name from Persia
myths.text: The Simurgh of Iranian tradition is one of the oldest great birds of world mythology. In the Avesta she roosts in the branches of the sacred tree; across Sogdian and Sasanian art she spreads composite wings over the Tree of Life; and in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh she rears the hero Zal and guides his son Rostam through every impossible task — part dog, part lion, part bird, and wholly wise. How her name crossed into Slavic as Simargl is the ordinary work of steppe history: Alanic- and Sarmatian-speaking peoples of the north Pontic steppe served as carriers, and a worn-down Simurgh entered East Slavic speech generations before a chronicler wrote it down. The borrowing tells its own myth: a god can be an import, and a pantheon a port — Kyiv's sky had been in conversation with Persia's for centuries before either had a church.

myths.title: Guardian of Seeds?
myths.text: Boris Rybakov, the most influential historian of Slavic religion, gave Simargl his modern job description: guardian of seeds and plant life. The argument runs on two legs — the Simurgh's Iranian role as protector of the Tree of Life and of vegetation, and the presence in Slavic folklore of the Sey Div, a chthonic being who guards sown fields and must be placated at sowing and harvest. If Simargl is a worn Simurgh, and the Sey Div is his folk memory in reverse, then the god who drowned in the Dnieper was the protector of every furrow in Rus'. The hypothesis is ingenious and untestable: no text calls Simargl a seed-guardian, and the Sey Div connection rests on names and functions, never on an attestation. It is cited here exactly as Rybakov framed it — a structure built from parallels, honest about its own materials, and better than any rival precisely because it admits what it is.

myths.title: The Sphinx of the Pantheon
myths.text: Like Stribog, Simargl must be described by what is missing. No treaty swears by him; the Malalas gloss that rescued Dažbog passes him by; no saint inherits his day; South Slavic folklore preserves no Dajbog-like fossil of his name; and no archaeological find — not the Zbruch idol, not the axe-amulets, not the Peryn' enclosure — can be tied to him with any confidence. What remains is structural: a pantheon needs a vegetation-guardian, the name is Iranian, and the Iranian original is the greatest plant-guardian of the Near Eastern myth-world. Modern scholarship has filled the gap with a functional god; modern paganism has filled it with a feathered angel of gardens. Both are guesses at a shape the sources never drew. Simargl is the Kyiv pantheon's sphinx: a riddle posed in a foreign accent, guarding a seed no one has ever seen.

lore.syncretism: Simargl is syncretism made flesh — or rather, made loanword. His entire existence in Rus' is the product of an intercultural translation: the Simurgh, grandmother-figure of Persian epic and guardian of the sacred tree, re-emerging on the Dnieper as a minor idol with a clipped name. Iranian studies have tracked his relatives across Sogdian silver, Sasanian stucco, and the Shahnameh; Slavic studies have tracked the reception — a name absorbed, declinable, and finally drowned. The Christian centuries had no use for him and no saint took his place, which is why no folk-fossil survives to compare with Dajbog or Sveti Vlaho. In the modern era the borrowing has run in reverse: fantasy fiction and Slavic Native Faith re-export Simargl toward his Iranian cousins, sometimes literally reuniting him with the Simurgh in games and novels — a reminder that gods, like names, travel, and the border between borrowing and genealogy is where most pantheons actually live.
lore.culturalLegacy: Simargl's legacy divides in two. Among Iranists he is a footnote in the biography of the Simurgh — evidence of how far the great bird's name flew, from Avestan hymns to a chronicle on the Dnieper. Among Slavists and the wider public he is the patron of gardens and sown fields, a role created almost entirely by Rybakov's twentieth-century reconstruction and embraced with enthusiasm by Rodnover communities, children's encyclopedias, and fantasy games, where winged guardians named Simargl recur from Minsk to the app stores. The historical god is a lesson in how reception manufactures memory: two lines of real evidence, a century of confident elaboration, and a deity who now feels as anciently Slavic as Perun — though his wings were grown on the Iranian plateau and only molted into Slavic on the way north.
lore.extendedMeditation: Simargl is a parable about what survives. Nothing of him survives — no story, no prayer, no image — except a name, and the name is a survivor twice over: the Simurgh outlived Zoroastrian empires to be sung by Ferdowsi, and then outlived the journey north to be drowned, once, in a river, by a chronicle that did not understand what it was erasing. We know him only as a translation — a word carried across languages and centuries until it meant less and stood for more. Moderns have given him back his wings, his seeds, his gardens; perhaps that is what translation always is, the endless human work of deciding what a worn-down name should guard. The Simurgh reared heroes; Simargl guards furrows; both are the same old impulse — to post a winged thing at the boundary between what we plant and what we fear. A god made entirely of borrowing teaches that no tradition is pure, and none the poorer for it.
lore.archaeology: No material evidence names or securely depicts Simargl. Candidates have been proposed — winged figures on medieval pendants, Tree-of-Life motifs on jewelry, the enigmatic four-sided Zbruch idol, more often assigned to Svetovit — but none carries an inscription, and the Iranian visual language he would have borrowed is precisely what Christian-era Rus' did not carve. The Kyiv hill of 988 has yielded no shrine deposit attributable to him. His 'archaeology' is therefore the archaeology of the steppe itself: Sarmatian and Alanic grave goods of the north Pontic region, with their Iranian animal-style art, supply the cultural bridge his name implies. The absence is itself informative — a vegetation-guardian's cult may have been domestic and unmonumental, kept in fields and storehouses rather than on hills, and such gods leave whorls, not walls.
